Title:
“UGAHacks Mini Olympics”

Goal:
Create a fun, low stress way for participants to take a break, meet new people, and build community during the hackathon.

Target audience:
All participants, especially those looking for a break from coding or wanting to meet new people.

Format:
A series of short, high energy mini games that people can join individually or in teams.

Structure:
Quick intro and grouping participants into teams
Rotate through different mini games such as a watermelon eating contest, cup stacking challenge, relay races, or trivia
Keep a simple point system for each activity
Final round with top teams competing in one last challenge
Announce winners and give out prizes

Resources needed:
Basic supplies for games like cups, food items, and small props
Volunteers to help run each station and keep score
Open space to host activities

Community engagement element:
Encourages people to meet teammates outside of their hack group
Creates a fun and memorable break from hacking
Offer small prizes like snacks, merch, or gift cards to keep energy high
Makes the event more inclusive for non technical participants who still want to be involved

Title: Pitch workshop with Speed Networking 
Goal: To smash the myth that hackers can’t sell products or be social. This event helps people meet new people and learn how to sell their product at the showcase.

The Setup:
Every participant receives a number at the door. The room is divided into numbered or labeled zones. Randomly assigned trios meet at their designated number.

The Outline:
0-5m: Quick-fire presentation on "How to sell an idea" with tips and tricks to help them during the presentation.

5-25m: The Sprints
Round 1: Each trio is given a random field (e.g., Healthcare) and a random topic (e.g., Wearable Tech).
The Prep (4 min): The trio must come up with a "product" and a pitch.
The Pitch (2 min): One person pitches to a circulating judge/organizer. Immediate feedback is given

The Intermission: A mandatory LinkedIn Swap break(to get those connection numbers up). Winner Announcement

Round 2: Numbers are shuffled, and the process repeats with new groups.

One project I took real ownership over was a Sentiment Analysis API that I built and deployed using Python, FastAPI, and Scikit-learn. The goal was to create a reliable service that could classify text sentiment in real time while handling real-world inputs and edge cases.

I approached the project by first building a machine learning pipeline using TF-IDF and Logistic Regression trained on a large IMDB dataset. From there, I designed a REST API with clear endpoints for predictions and batch processing, and implemented Pydantic validation to ensure clean and consistent input handling. I also added a confidence threshold system so the API could return “uncertain” for low-confidence predictions, which made the system more realistic and robust.

To make sure the project was fully complete and production-ready, I wrote a pytest suite with over 20 tests covering edge cases and validation, and set up a deployment pipeline that automatically retrained the model on deploy. I also created a simple demo interface to make the API easier to interact with. Throughout the process, I iterated based on testing and debugging, and made sure each component—from the model to the API to deployment—was reliable and well-integrated.

Real-Time Data Streaming Workshop!

Windowing (tumbling vs sliding windows), statefulness (remembering what happened earlier to make a decision now).
Producer (source of data), broker (Kafka or something similar), consumer (code that reacts to the data).

Part 3: Live Build
1.	Use a live API like Coinbase API for crypto prices or OpenSky for live aircraft positions.

Workshop Title: CAD for Hackers: Designing Custom Hardware Enclosures
Objective: To teach participants how to turn their projects into a professional, finished product using Fusion 360 for 3D-printable housing.

I. Introduction (5 minutes)
The "Finished Product" Mindset: Why a custom enclosure matters for durability, portability, and judge appeal at a hackathon.

Background: Briefly share a profressionals experience as an Autodesk Certified User and how mechanical design bridges the gap between software and the physical world.

II. Fusion 360 Foundations (15 minutes)
Sketching & Constraints: How to create accurate 2D footprints for common components (Arduinos, ESP32s, sensors).

The "Box" Method: Creating the base shell using extrusions and the "Shell" tool to save time.

Component Clearances: Why adding a 0.2mm - 0.4mm tolerance is the difference between a part that fits and a part that snaps.

III. Design for Assembly (15 minutes)
Mounting Logic: How to design "standoffs" or snap-fit clips so the electronics stay secure without needing messy glue.

Ports & Ventilation: Cutting holes for USB-C cables, power switches, and cooling vents using the "Combine/Cut" features.

Fasteners: Choosing between M3 screws or simple friction-fit lids for quick access.

IV. The Aesthetic Edge (10 minutes)
Visual Polish: Using fillets and chamfers to give the design a sleek, ergonomic look rather than a basic cube.

Branding: How to "emboss" or "engrave" team names or project logos directly into the 3D model for that extra professional touch.

V. From Screen to Printer (10 minutes)
Exporting for Success: Preparing STLs and choosing the right orientation to minimize print time. 

Troubleshooting: Real-world advice on what to do when a print fails or a measurement is slightly off.

VI. Q&A and Demo (5 minutes)
Open floor for specific project questions and a quick look at some of the complex assemblies you’ve worked on in your aerospace coursework or internship.

Event Title: "The Perfect Pour": A Hands-On Craft Coffee Workshop

Type: Interactive Skill-Building / Fueling Station

Goal: To teach hackers the science of the pour-over while providing a high-quality caffeine boost to clear the "coding fog."

Outline:

The Synchronized Setup (30 mins): We arrange the room into "Brewing Stations." Each station is equipped with a plastic dripper, paper filters, a mug, and a pre-measured portion of freshly ground beans.

Guided Instruction (45 mins): * The Bloom: The group is led through the "bloom" phase, explaining the importance of degassing coffee for better flavor (a perfect parallel to "debugging" code).

The Pour: A step-by-step follow-along where participants practice their pouring technique using shared gooseneck kettles at each table.

Customization & Alt-Fuel: For those who don't drink coffee, we provide the exact same setup but with high-quality loose-leaf teas or offer complimentary energy drinks at the "Tech-Fuel" sideboard so everyone can participate in the social break.

Logistics & Supply Management:

Inventory: Will have to manage the procurement of bulk filters, 50+ compostable cups, and enough kettles to ensure a 1:4 kettle-to-student ratio.

Water Station: A centralized "Hot Water Refill" zone to keep the workshop moving efficiently.

Waste & Cleanup: Since this is "hands-on," we'll set up designated bins for wet filters and coffee grounds to ensure the hacking space remains pristine.

Contingency: If the venue has strict "heating" rules, we pivot to a "Cold Brew Mixology" workshop using pre-steeped concentrates where hackers learn to balance acidity and sweetness using different ratios and syrups.

column32: My AI Cookbook is the one. I came up with the idea, built it from scratch, and shipped it, no team, no one telling me what to do next. The idea was simple and something my friends and I have needed for a while. You tell it what ingredients you have, it selects a recipe using those and then constructs a user friends output with instructions and steps. The hard part was making the AI outputs actually reliable. Early on, the Gemini API would return malformed JSON or hallucinate ingredients that weren't in the input, and I had to build structured prompt engineering and parsing logic to catch and correct that across 50+ edge cases I tested myself. I designed the REST API with FastAPI, handled the backend data pipelines in Python, and deployed the whole thing on render where I let users test it. I onboarded about 50+ users, collected feedback, identified what was breaking, and shipped fixes in iterations. If something was broken, it was on me to figure out why and fix it. That's the kind of ownership I'm looking for more of, and why I want to be on the UGAHacks tech team.

Workshop Title: Career Prep for Hackathons — Resume, Networking & Interviews
- Goal: Help participants present themselves effectively for internships, jobs, and networking opportunities
- Format: Workshop + interactive stations + mock practice

I. Agenda
1. Resume Review Basics (20 min)
- What recruiters look for (clarity, impact, relevance)
- How to structure a strong resume:
- Experience (impact-focused bullet points)
- Projects (hackathon-friendly format)

Skills section 
- Common mistakes: Too vague / no metrics + Listing duties instead of impact
- Mini activity: Convert a weak bullet point → strong bullet point

2. Networking Skills (20 min)
- What networking actually means (not “being fake”)
- How to introduce yourself in 30 seconds: Name + major + interest + goal
- How to keep conversations going: Asking meaningful questions / Finding common ground (projects, interests, hackathon work)
- Do’s and don’ts of networking
- Activity: Pair practice: 2-minute networking conversations

3. Interview Preparation (20–25 min)
- Types of interviews:
+ Behavioral
+ Technical / case-based (depending on field)
+ STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result)
- Common questions: “Tell me about yourself” / “Why this role?” / “Tell me about a challenge you faced”
- Mini mock interview in pairs or small groups

4. Hackathon-Specific Career Strategy (10–15 min)
- How to present hackathon projects on resume:
- Focus on impact + outcome
- Highlight teamwork and technical tools
- How to talk about hackathon experience in interviews
- Turning hackathon work into internship opportunities

5. Q&A / Open Networking (10 min)
- Participants ask questions
- Optional networking time with mentors or organizers

II. Materials Needed
- Resume examples (good vs bad)
- Networking script template
- STAR method worksheet
- Project/resume template (Google Doc or Notion)

Well I love RL so I’ll use that as an example. Imagine a n-many player game of battleship where each player can choose to attack only one of the players present. 

Each team may submit an algorithm for choosing the placement of and targeting for their battleships. I would give them some abstract functions to implement (input the number of ships remaining and location of hits/misses for each player). 

Players would have a certain amount of time (half of the event?) to create their algorithms. Then for the rest of the event, we can show how the game is progressing on a screen, where we time it to finish at the end of the hackathon. 

This multiplayer version is not a solved game to my knowledge, so it should prove a challenge both time wise and approach wise. They could skip rl and use a fixed policy, they could implement a if-else based policy, they could treat it as a MARL problem (though questionable if they have time to run that).

In my my internship at sports licensing solutions (forgot to list it on my resume) I was the only developer with knowledge spanning python, excel, computer vision, so I solved many small tasks.

One particularly fun story was they wanted to visually identify different sports team logos on rubber mats. This was fairly challenging as they wanted “100% accuracy” (a unicorn in ai) and they had over 300 distinct teams they wanted to identify between.

After much tinkering, I used a cool trick applicable in the real world, I made the training set my testing set! This is counterintuitive to most ML, but in this instance it is exactly what I needed. I constructed a light box with a very controlled scene to ensure reproducible images, and I made a tool to ensure proper rotation of the mat. The I was able to achieve 100% accuracy by intentionally overfitting to my physically constrained space of mat images!
